Spirit, you speak of neighbours I have not met. Where is this Wewush? How many mouths hunger there? We have grain in our granary, yes, enough for the planting season and the lean months ahead. But I do not know these people. Are they farmers who lost their crop, or hunters with empty hands? If I send my people walking with heavy baskets, will they return with thanks, or will they find only empty bellies waiting to take what is ours? Tell me more, or be silent. I do not give away the seed of my children's winter bread for a whisper in the dark.

Spirit, I hear you. I do not know these Wewush folk, nor the ground they walk upon. You say they hunger, yet winter follows spring, and grain is the wall between life and hard death when the cold winds come.  

Where do they dwell? Can we reach them in a day's walk? I am warm to strangers, and no child should cry from an empty belly, but I will not pour out our winter breath for a voice in the dark. Show us the path to their doors, or let their own feet carry them here to ask with open hands. Then we will weigh what is fair to share.

The wind I know. It comes heavy off the sea, it flaps the hides of our tents, it dries the nets. Yet in all my years it has never stopped to ask me its own name. So, voice—if you are indeed a spirit and not the fancy of a full belly—tell me why you trouble my sleep now. Our people are joyful, our xi wheat is stored. What do you seek? I am listening, but I am not bound to heed.

You say they hunger, but I have only your dream-word for it, and spirits do not always speak straight. We have grain in the granary, yes, but we also have twelve children to raise and winter is a hard creditor who never forgets a debt. Where do these people dwell? How many mouths do they feed? What do they offer in return? If they are real and truly in need, let them come to our fire, or let me send men to look upon their faces. I do not give wheat to strangers on the whisper of a ghost.

I know the wind. It blows off the water and tugs at the tent hides. But wind has no mouth, and it does not ask to be known. You speak like a person, not like air. So tell me plainly: why have you come? We have planting to finish and fish to dry. If you know something useful for my people, say it now. If not, I will wake and think on grain and nets, and leave you to the sky where you belong.

We have xi wheat in good store—our granary is heavy—but grain is the breath that carries a village through the lean months. To pour it into hands I do not know is no small thing. Are these people who would trade fair and bind friendship, or are they thieves and takers? Speak plain, for I must fill the mouths I know before I fill strange ones.

Spirit, I do not know Joawethom. My people have walked far in every season and found no such village. You are one voice without a face, without a footprint. I do not give grain to shadows.

If these neighbours are real and their hunger is true, that is a hard thing. We are not tight-fisted with strangers. But winter comes for us too, and our stores must carry our own through the lean months. I will not send wheat on the word of a dream alone.

Tell me where they dwell, how many mouths they have, and how you came to see their empty bellies. Give me something my own eyes can follow, or my own messengers can find. Then I will weigh your words. Until then, you may be nothing but wind.

You move over my roofs—what do you carry to me? The planting moon is rising, and the fields wait for seed. If you are the wind, you have seen much. Speak plain, then. What truth do you bring that my eyes cannot see?

You speak of Joawethom. I do not know this name. Our hunters have not sat by their fires, nor have our scouts seen smoke from their roofs.

You may see far, spirit, or you may see false. I have learned that a dream is one voice only, and voices in darkness sometimes lie. We have wheat in the granary, yes, but winter follows spring like shadow follows sun. I will not give away the mouths of my children for words alone.

How do you know their stomachs are empty? Have you walked their fields and seen the bare earth? Did you count their store pits and find them hollow?

If Joawethom truly starves, let their feet walk here, or let ours walk there with eyes open. Let us see thin faces and empty hands, not just hear whispers in sleep. Then, being fair people, we will share what we can spare. Until then, the grain stays under lock and our own people come first.

The meat in our stores runs thin—only sixteen weeks of it. And the ground stands empty while spring grows old. We eat fish and gathered plants, but grain is the backbone that carries a village through the white months.

If you speak true about the rain, then yes, we must plant. But I have seen dry summers kill shoots in the earth. Why do you push us to risk our xi wheat now, rather than wait to see if the clouds gather?

I know the wind. It tugs at our hide tents and carries salt from the great water. But many voices come in dreams, and not all speak true. You are one voice among many. If you carry word of the hunt, or the harvest to come, or what lies past the eastern hills, then speak it plain. Otherwise, why trouble my sleep when the planting season is upon us and my people have work?

You have blown over this village since before my grandfather's grandfather raised his first tent. What do you carry on your back that needs my ear tonight?
